title: Your Parser Already Knows Which Tokens Matter
hook: Constrained decoding tracks grammar state to keep JSON valid. PASK reuses that same signal to decide what to keep in the KV cache — and a wrong field is a failed tool call, not a stylistic blemish.
key_points: Structured generation (JSON, SQL, function calls) already runs a parser to enforce formal validity during decoding.
Parser transitions reveal which tokens carry schema-critical decisions: required fields, arguments, structural boundaries.
PASK turns that structure into layer-group-specific KV persistence decisions, which prior compression ignored.
Task-error sensitivity sets minimum protection floors; attention-output distortion allocates the remaining KV budget.
At a 0.33 KV budget on Qwen3-4B it beats the strongest compressed baseline by 17.4 points across eight BFCL subcategories.
End-to-end serving: up to 2.2x throughput, 3.3x lower time-per-output-token, at 0.53x the peak memory of full KV.
content_html: LLM agents live or die on structured output: JSON payloads, SQL, function calls. One wrong field and the downstream action fails. Constrained decoding already handles formal validity by running a grammar parser alongside generation. Wu and Chen noticed that the parser is also emitting a signal nobody was using — it knows which tokens are deciding required fields, argument values, and structural boundaries.
extra_html:
The method

PASK (Parser-Aware Structural KV Persistence) turns those parser transitions into per-layer-group decisions about which KV entries to keep. Two signals drive the allocation: task-error sensitivity sets minimum protection floors for positions where a mistake breaks the call, and attention-output distortion distributes whatever cache budget is left. An offline calibration stage compiles this into a persistence policy, so the runtime cost is a lightweight structure-conditioned lookup rather than online analysis.

Results

On Qwen3-4B at a 0.33 total KV budget, PASK reports a 17.4-point average gain over the strongest compressed baseline across eight BFCL non-live and Live subcategories. In end-to-end serving the authors report up to 2.2x higher throughput and 3.3x lower time-per-output-token while using about half the peak GPU memory of full KV.

The broader idea is worth keeping: when a task has structure the system is already computing, that structure is a better compression prior than generic attention statistics.

related.title: KV Cache Eviction, Formalized
related.hook: Everyone drops KV cache entries with clever heuristics. Formalize the problem properly and it turns into expectation estimation — which finally lets you correct for what you threw away.

flashcards.prompt: What free signal does PASK exploit that ordinary KV compression ignores?
flashcards.back_html: The parser state from constrained decoding. It is already being tracked to enforce grammar validity, and it says which tokens participate in schema-critical decisions.

flashcards.prompt: Why is structure-aware KV compression especially valuable for agents?

choices.text: One wrong field in a function call makes the downstream action fail outright
Agents generate far longer outputs than chat models
Tool calls cannot be produced with a compressed cache at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Structured output is brittle in a way prose is not — errors are not graded, they are execution failures. So compression should protect schema-critical positions preferentially.
